question: A consultancy team on an Enterprise plan wants Claude's research on a client sector to draw on the firm's own past engagement reports, not only on public material. What is the most appropriate approach?
options: A) Paste the single most relevant engagement report into each new chat whenever it seems likely to be needed.
B) Put the past engagement reports into the project so every research chat in it works from that material.
C) Ask Claude to describe what a firm like this one would probably have learned in past engagements.
D) Summarise the past engagement reports into a single page and rely on that page from then onwards.
correct_answers: B) Put the past engagement reports into the project so every research chat in it works from that material.
explanations: Relying on someone to notice the right report and paste it in means the internal evidence is used inconsistently. It also limits each piece of research to one report when the value lies in the pattern across many.

Correct. Project knowledge is durable background for every chat in that project, so the firm's own engagement history informs each piece of research without anyone re-pasting it. That makes the internal evidence a standing input rather than something remembered on a good day.

Asking Claude what such a firm would probably have learned invites it to invent the firm's experience. The reports exist and can be supplied, so guessing at their contents is the one option that produces confident fiction.

A single summary page discards the detail that makes past engagements useful, and it becomes stale the moment new work is completed. The team would be researching against a snapshot rather than the record.
